endorsements.quote: For clinicians, unlearning events should resemble any other regulated model update rather than a mysterious back-end process.
None of this is possible without ba sic infrastructure: a model registry, robust data lineage, versioned datasets and models, and append-only audit logs.
Teams must track where each training example influences deployed models, maintain version control for models and datasets, and reserve compute fo r deletion and re validation.

Organisations should define a clear chain of responsibility (e.g. Clinical AI Safety Lead plus designated committee) and written criteria for when unlearning is triggered and what evidence is required.

For closed -source, vendor -hosted models, deploying organisations have no access to weights and might require attestations or technical evidence from AI vendors that models can honour data deletion requests, as part of procurement or approval.
Failed validation should trigger rollback and escalation to a clinical AI safety committee.

unlisted_practices: Design high-risk clinical AI so that targeted remediation of learned data influence is feasible where legal, ethical, community-governance, or clinical-safety grounds require removal or correction.
Define a small number of clear unlearning triggers and pre-register a validation plan for each, specifying metrics, subgroups, and non-inferiority margins.

Run a pre-specified post-unlearning validation battery (discrimination, calibration, key subgroups, membership inference where feasible) after each unlearning event, with thresholds for absolute floors and tolerable relative degradation.

Require unlearning-readiness in procurement, including dataset manifest, consent and licence status, model registry, declared unlearning approach with assurance target, and operational service levels.
Publish clinician-facing revision notes in EHRs explaining what changed, why, and with what effect on performance and calibration after unlearning events.
Select the unlearning method by model type and risk, defaulting to full retraining for small or high-risk models where feasible and designing for partitioning when frequent deletions are expected.
Consider retrieval-augmented architectures for consent-sensitive or frequently changing patient data where clinical performance permits.
Consider model retirement or disgorgement where assurance thresholds for unlearning cannot be met.
Designate an authority to decide whether a deletion request is legitimate, which models it affects, and what performance degradation is tolerable.
Make unlearning requirements proportionate, risk-based, and supported by shared infrastructure such as procurement templates and assurance test batteries.

screen.reason: This is a viewpoint/commentary article arguing for machine unlearning as a governance requirement for clinical AI deployment.
